This is a result of the commissioning of the next generation of nuclear power stations and a decrease in power demand, offsetting the requirements for gas-fired generation. Decarbonisation agenda The lack of political consensus for centralised carbon reduction policy restricts the emergence of large scale low carbon and renewable technologies such as CCS and marine. tavily_results.content:
Innovation is critical to helping us meet the challenges of transitioning to a zero carbon future. As we sit at the very heart of the energy system, we play a central role in overcoming these challenges.

Read the story of how the we have decarbonised the electricity system to date, offering a blueprint to other countries around the world to help them reduce emissions.

All of our projects contribute towards our effort to make the grid ready to operate with 100% zero carbon electricity by 2025.

# STC New Modification Proposal Submission Date - 10 November 2026 [...] Our energy system is complex, with an increasing number of interconnections. This means that disruption to one part can have implications for another. But this complexity also provides us with more options to mitigate problems.

We will develop comprehensive and independent insights across the entire energy system, offering clear recommendations to policy makers, industry decision makers and leadership across our organisation on how to accelerate energy transition progress.

Whether you’re interested in the innovation underway in the Markets team or are looking to brush up on market fundamentals, you’ve come to the right place. [...] Security of Supply analyses where the energy we need over the short, medium and long-term will come from. In doing so it assesses a wide range of factors that could affect our supply of energy, enabling early actions and decisions to ensure we can meet future demand.

From hospitals to households, telecoms to transportation, our society relies on electricity. Our control centre makes sure there is always a reliable and safe supply as we move megawatts around the country.

We will deliver efficient system access for Generation and Demand projects, so that those projects that are first ready can be first served – delivering the energy system to meet net zero and facilitating economic growth by connecting new and existing industries.

tavily_results.title: Coal to clean – the UK's decarbonisation story | National Energy System Operator
tavily_results.content:
We are working with the Powering Past Coal Alliance, GO15 and the newly formed Global Power System Transformation Consortium to do just that. Through these international organisations we can share our knowledge and expertise with system operators, regulators, legislators, and policy makers across the world, helping each other on our decarbonisation journey.

We’ve proved that you can take an energy system with little renewable generation and transform it into a cleaner and greener system with deliverable plans for zero carbon operation.

I look forward to sharing more of this with you over the coming year. [...] This variability of renewables means that we need robust operability plans to ensure they can be utilised when they are available, and we have alternatives when they are not.

We’ve achieved this by developing new services, provided by both fossil fuel and renewable generators. These services support the network, enabling it to adapt to fluctuations in supply from renewables.

Today our greatest challenge is shifting the provision of these services from fossil fuel generators to renewable sources – many have doubted that this could be done. [...] Providing connections to the network for renewables is not straightforward. Generators usually connect to the network on the basis that they can reach maximum output at any time – so the network is reinforced in their local area accordingly. However, with wind this is not the case.

If we approached wind in the same way as gas, we would overbuild the network. Therefore, in some areas, we allow wind to connect without undertaking the wider network reinforcements. This means we occasionally have to restrict output from wind generation, but it is a lower cost than building the transmission assets. This flexible approach promotes decarbonisation while protecting consumers from unnecessary costs.

local_documents.snippet: Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany This study estimates the health burden in Germany caused by long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 emissions from hard coal- and lignite-fired power plants in 2015. The authors focus on source-specific disease burden rather than total air pollution, asking how much disease could be attributed specifically to emissions from these coal power plants. The central conclusion is that both hard coal and lignite contributed a measurable burden of disease, with lignite producing the larger impact for both pollutants. The methodology combines air pollution modeling, population exposure assessment, and health burden calculation. local_documents.snippet: to Ambient PM2.5 Mortality This paper provides a global assessment of which sectors and fuels contribute most to ambient PM2.5 exposure and PM2.5-attributable mortality. The motivation is practical: fine particulate matter is the world's leading environmental health risk, but effective air quality policy requires knowing which sources drive the burden in different places. The study covers 21 world regions, 204 countries, and 200 sub-national areas, allowing comparison across global, national, and urban-relevant scales. The methodology combines atmospheric modeling, satellite-based exposure estimates, emissions inventories, and disease-specific health risk functions. The authors ran 24 sensitivity simulations with the GEOS-Chem global chemical transport model to estimate source and fuel contributions. It begins from the position that the country has already reduced many of the worst pollution problems through regulation, industrial investment, and a cleaner energy mix, but that air pollution remains one of the UK's largest public health challenges. The strategy stresses that harmful emissions now come from many diffuse sources, not only from large factories or road traffic. The document identifies air pollution as a result of how the UK generates power, heats homes, produces food, manufactures goods, and moves people and freight. local_documents.snippet: ticles are recognized as important concerns, but the evidence was not sufficient to derive full quantitative air quality guideline values. WHO recommends monitoring, exposure assessment, source control where possible, and risk communication for these particle types. Implementation is presented as a policy process, not just a measurement exercise. Countries are encouraged to assess national needs and capacity, translate the guideline levels into enforceable standards where appropriate, build air quality management systems, and use health risk assessment to compare policy options. WHO stresses the role of the health sector in synthesizing evidence, communicating risks, monitoring impacts, and supporting decision-making, while also making clear that air pollution control requires cooperation across transport, energy, housing, industry, agriculture, urban planning, and environmental agencies
